title: Loving strangers
hook: in several traditions, the stranger is a test of love

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was loving children: love that gives freely and holds loosely. Your line was through you, not from you.

Who was the last stranger to do something kind for you? Someone who held a door with a foot while juggling groceries. A driver who waved you into traffic. A person on a train who pointed out that your bag was open. They may never turn up again, and they didn't need anything back. Strangers are the people love has the least reason to reach: no history, no debt, no family tie. That's exactly why several ancient texts made the stranger a test.
screen: `THE LAST STRANGER WHO WAS KIND.` → `NO HISTORY, NO DEBT.` → `WHY THE STRANGER IS A TEST.`

segments.voice: First, Abraham runs to the strangers. In Genesis, Abraham is sitting at the door of his tent in the heat of the day when he sees three men standing nearby. He doesn't wait to find out who they are. He runs to meet them, bows, and asks them to stay. Then he hurries: water for their feet, fresh bread, a calf prepared, food set before them while he stands by. The chapter opens by telling the reader that the LORD appeared to Abraham there; how much Abraham himself understood at first, the text leaves open. Second, ye were strangers. Leviticus doesn't just say tolerate the outsider: "thou shalt love him as thyself; for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt." The reason given is memory. You know what it's like to be the outsider. Third, angels unawares. The letter to the Hebrews has a line in which some readers hear Abraham's story: "Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares." The Greeks had their own version: in Homer's Odyssey, a princess tells her frightened friends that strangers and beggars come from Zeus. Fourth, a smile is small hospitality. Not everyone has a tent or a calf to offer. But hospitality comes in small sizes: eye contact with the cashier, patience with a lost tourist, a nod to the new person at work. These texts treat the stranger not as a risk to manage but as someone to welcome, with common sense about safety. Here, the stranger is where love reaches past loyalty.
screen: `ABRAHAM RUNS TO THE STRANGERS.` · `YE WERE STRANGERS.` · `ANGELS UNAWARES.` · `A SMILE IS SMALL HOSPITALITY.` · then, large: `THE STRANGER.`

segments.voice: Let a stranger who once did something kind for you come back to mind, a door held, a wave into traffic, directions on a strange street, and stay with that moment for a few breaths. Let the thanks you never got to say be said silently now. If you pray, you can give thanks for that stranger before God, nameless as they are.
Loving strangers. Welcome offered to people with no claim on you, the way Abraham ran to his guests and Leviticus says to love the outsider as yourself. Today's word.
Your line: the stranger. Every one of us has been the outsider somewhere. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Jews and Christians read Abraham's welcome of three guests in Genesis 18 as a model of hospitality, and the Torah commands love for the stranger; hospitality to guests and travelers is also honored in other faiths and cultures.

chat.says: Why would old scriptures care so much about being kind to strangers?
options: Leviticus gives memory as the reason: ye were strangers in Egypt, so love the outsider.
Because strangers were always angels in disguise, so it was safer to be polite.
Because the law only asked people to tolerate outsiders, never to love them.
chat.meaning: Leviticus says to love the stranger as thyself, for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt. You know what it's like to be the outsider.

notes: Audit pass (serious): Genesis 18:1 tells the reader at the outset that 'the LORD appeared unto him', so 'only later does the story reveal who his guests were' was wrong, and the myth/fork claimed Abraham acted 'before he knows', which the text does not say (readers differ on what Abraham recognized, e.g. his 'My Lord' in 18:3). Teach, myth and fork reveal corrected; the narrator's closing verdict on what love 'really' is was softened.
The outline hook ('the stranger is the oldest test in many traditions') is softened to 'several traditions' and 'oldest' is dropped under the claims rule.

Hebrews 13:2 echoing Genesis 18 is a common reading, not stated in the text itself; the script says 'some readers hear Abraham's story' in it.
